title: 12-DOF Quadruped Robotic Platform
summary: Design and pre-fabrication validation of a 12-DOF quadruped through CAD, structural analysis, inverse kinematics, gait simulation, and IMU posture stabilization.

body.title: Download the full design validation report (PDF)

children.text: The four legs are arranged symmetrically, with three degrees of freedom per leg. The chassis keeps the center of mass near the middle, and the gait shifts it toward the supporting legs before lifting a foot.
The Fusion 360 assembly places the legs symmetrically around a central chassis.

image.alt: Quadruped CAD model from multiple viewpoints
image.caption: Quadruped CAD model from multiple viewpoints

children.text: The SolidWorks static model used an acrylic base plate, PLA structural members and fixed supports at the legs. Gravity represented the load from the robot and its electronics. The greatest displacement reported was about 1.77 mm near the middle of the base plate. The factor-of-safety study provides a baseline for deciding where to reinforce the prototype.

children.text: The MATLAB tool maps requested foot positions to joint angles and checks them against servo limits. It marks unreachable poses in red.

children.text: A single-leg URDF model was used in PyBullet to check that the joint commands calculated by inverse kinematics move the simulated leg as intended.
The free-base simulation checked whether the robot could hold its standing posture within the modeled MG996R servo torque limits.

Before each swing, the controller shifts the center of mass toward the supporting legs to make the continuous crawl more stable on flat ground.

children.text: The simulated IMU reports orientation and angular velocity. Feedback from it drives vertical leg corrections that stabilize roll and pitch during walking and turning.

children.text: The report records simulation validation for structural FEA, inverse kinematics, single-leg motion, standing, forward crawl, turning, the combined simulator, and simulated IMU feedback for roll and pitch.

title: GeoNavigator
summary: An ESP32 robot that follows waypoints from a browser interface and estimates its position with wheel encoders and an IMU.

coverImage.alt: GeoNavigator robot with its decorated top, acrylic chassis, wheels, and exposed electronics
coverImage.caption: Cover image from the GeoNavigator video demo.

children.text: A small robot that can navigate to coordinates using dead reckoning. Built for a robotics project.

body.title: GeoNavigator demo
body.summary: The robot traces a square, triangle, circle, and the Ursa Minor constellation.

children.text: Drives to waypoints you set on a web interface
Tracks position using wheel encoders + gyro
Hosts its own WiFi so you can control it from your phone/laptop
N20 Gear Motors with Encoders (x2) - 6V, 200RPM, 50:1 ratio

title: ODIN – Productivity & Task Management System
summary: A keyboard-first web workspace for tasks, goals, calendar events, focus sessions, and personal notes.

coverImage.alt: ODIN Command Center with sidebar navigation, task count, upcoming event, and goal progress
coverImage.caption: Dashboard from the ODIN video demo.

children.text: ODIN is a productivity-focused web application designed to help users organize tasks, goals, schedules, and personal notes in one centralized workspace. The project focuses on creating a lightweight and fast productivity environment with keyboard-first workflows and an intuitive dashboard.

ODIN acts as a personal productivity hub where users can manage their daily work, track goals, schedule events, and maintain personal notes. The system combines multiple productivity tools into a single interface to reduce friction when managing different aspects of personal organization.
Create tasks quickly using a simple interface
Track upcoming tasks from the dashboard
Track goals alongside tasks and other productivity items
Organized goal tracking within the dashboard
Upcoming events are displayed directly on the dashboard
